title: Semi-supervised Multi-view Clustering with Active Constraints

problem.claim: Multi-view clustering needs to use weak pairwise supervision information available in real applications.

gap.claim: Most existing multi-view clustering approaches are purely unsupervised and ignore weak supervision information such as active queries.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes SMCAC, a semi-supervised multi-view clustering method with active constraints.
SMCAC uses a tensor-based multi-view graph learning model with sample pairwise-constraint regularization and an alternating-direction-minimization optimization algorithm.
SMCAC actively selects uncertain or difficult sample pairs using divergence among multi-view similarities, and alternates clustering with querying until the maximum query count is reached.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments on several popular datasets validate the effectiveness of SMCAC.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-view clustering has received increasing attention.
Existing approaches are mostly unsupervised and overlook weak supervision obtainable through active queries.
The paper proposes SMCAC to use weak pairwise constraints for improved clustering.
The method alternates tensor-based constrained graph learning and active selection of uncertain sample pairs, supported by an optimization algorithm.
The authors report effectiveness on several popular datasets.

source_observation.claim: The method alternates between learning a constrained multi-view clustering model and querying uncertain sample pairs.

interpretation.claim: Iterative interaction between model uncertainty and targeted supervision can focus limited queries on difficult cases.

application.claim: Use disagreement or divergence across views to prioritize human or oracle feedback when supervision is costly.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how query cost, noisy constraints, or view disagreement affect performance.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not describe the maximum number of queries or the computational complexity of the optimization algorithm.
The abstract does not establish robustness to noisy, contradictory, or incomplete pairwise constraints.
